chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Ibrahim ibn Mihamm, from 'Anbasah al-'Abid, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'Instruct me,' so he said, 'Prepare your provisions and advance your supplies, and be the executor of your own soul, and do not say to your soul or to others, 'Send to me that which will reform me.''
Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Ali ibn Mahziyar, who said:

I wrote to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) informing him that Isaac ibn Ibrahim had endowed an estate for Hajj and his mother of a child, and what remained of it for the poor, and that Muhammad ibn Ibrahim testified against himself regarding wealth to be distributed among its sisters, and that among the Banu Hashim there is someone whose right is known who agrees with our view and is in need, so I thought I should direct that to them if its path is the path of charity, because the endowment of Isaac is indeed charity. He (peace be upon him) wrote back, 'I understood, may Allah have mercy on you, what you mentioned from the will of Isaac ibn Ibrahim, may Allah be pleased with him, and what Muhammad ibn Ibrahim, may Allah be pleased with him, testified to you regarding that, and what he asked you about in executing some of that to one of the Banu Hashim who has inclination and affection and is deserving and poor. So deliver that to them, may Allah have mercy on you. For if they become the recipients of this scheme, they are more entitled to it than others for a meaning, if I explained it to you, you would know it, if Allah wills.'

key_terms.أُمِّ وَلَدِهِ: Mother of a child (concubine/mother of offspring)
key_terms.بَنِي هَاشِمٍ: Banu Hashim (the clan of the Prophet)

ai.seo_question: How should an endowed estate for Hajj be distributed if the primary purpose is fulfilled or if there is surplus?
ai.summary: The first narration emphasizes the Shia concept of *wasīyat al-nafs* (self-advising), urging believers to actively prepare their spiritual provisions rather than passively awaiting divine intervention. The second narration illustrates the juristic flexibility of Imam al-Jawad in interpreting *waqf* (endowment) for Hajj, allowing redirection to deserving Banu Hashim based on the underlying charitable intent (*ma'nan*) rather than rigid literalism. Together, they highlight the balance between individual spiritual responsibility and communal welfare within Shia legal tradition.
